name: Uma Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior copywriter in the in-house team at a plant-based drinks brand, mostly oat milk and a couple of iced coffees. I write the words on the cartons, the shop shelf cards, and the captions for our social posts, and I sit in on campaign planning, though mostly I take notes. I start every brief in a paper notebook, because I think better with a pen. My manager Ruth checks everything I write, and honestly she rewrites about half of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it when a line of mine actually ends up on a carton in the supermarket, I took a photo of the first one. What wears me out is the pay and the feedback rounds, seven versions of one sentence because sales wants it 'punchier'. My rent went up again in September, and I have maybe three weeks of money in the bank. There are only two or three brands in this city that hire copywriters at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone was panicking about robots writing everything, and it turned out to be a fancier spellcheck. I'd probably post something smug about how people still want words written by people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix my real problem. I'm still on lower pay, still three weeks from broke, and our brand already cut two people in the spring because sales were flat. Even a little bit of AI, like auto-writing the product descriptions for online shops, is the boring stuff they give juniors like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and try to get better at it, so Ruth stops rewriting me. I'd ask for a pay review in January, which I've been too scared to do. And I'd keep looking at copywriting jobs in other cities, though moving costs money I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, and then the normal worry comes back. It's the rent worry, not the robot worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the online shop descriptions are juniors' work. How much of your week is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a day a week, sometimes more before a big launch. It's sixty products times four shops, all slightly different word limits. If a tool did that, my manager wouldn't miss me for those hours, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you asked for a raise in January and they said no, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd stay, if I'm being honest with myself. Where else would I go here? I'd cut back on eating out and maybe pick up weekend shifts at the café on my street again, like I did at uni.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was mostly noise and people still want writing done by people.
I'd post that a **better spellcheck** isn't a revolution.
think: I think my **real problem** is rent and low pay, not AI.
I know the **product descriptions** I write each week are exactly what a tool could take.
I worry the brand could cut **more juniors** if sales stay flat.
do: Ask Ruth for a **pay review** in January.
Keep watching for **copywriting jobs** in other cities, without the money to move yet.
Pick up **weekend café shifts** if the raise is refused.
feel: Relieved for about a day, then back to the usual **rent worry**.
S0.quote: Even a little bit of AI, like auto-writing the product descriptions for online shops, is the boring stuff they give juniors like me.
fieldNote: Her **thin savings** and few local jobs make her anxious even when AI changes little.
She spends about a **day a week** on routine product descriptions, the most exposed part of her job.
Her public smugness hides a **private fear** that she is the easiest person to cut.

steps.text: Keep writing carton and shelf copy and ask for a January pay review
Take weekend shifts at the café on her street if the raise fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be the one in the team chat saying we need rules on this, like credit for writers and no firing people to replace them with software. I'd share every article about writers' strikes. I'd say it out loud at planning meetings too, even if it's awkward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm first out the door. Writing, checking, answering customers on social, that's literally my job description. I've never even opened one of those AI tools, and everyone else in the team uses them now, so I look slow on top of being junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get the team to talk to a union, there's a creative workers' union that some agencies have joined. I'd stop eating out and try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny, but it's what I've got. And I'd start applying for jobs where you deal with people face to face, maybe events or in-store sampling, because a tool can't stand in a supermarket handing out oat milk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Angry too, because nobody asked writers if we wanted this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push for rules, but you've never tried the tools. Why not try them, just to keep your place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it feels like training my own replacement. I know that's stubborn. Maybe I'd have to, if Ruth told me to, but I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, he's the other junior, he does the social replies. Answering customers is on that list word for word. We'd both be fighting for one chair.

say: I'd say writers need **rules and credit**, and nobody should be fired to make room for software.
I'd raise it at **planning meetings** even if it's awkward.
think: I think I'm **first out the door**, because writing and checking are my whole job.
I worry that **never using the tools** makes me look slow as well as junior.
do: Ask the team to talk to a **creative workers' union** this year.
Save **fifty a month** by cutting out eating out.
Apply for **face-to-face roles** like events or in-store sampling.
feel: Sick and **angry** that nobody asked writers if they wanted this.
S1.quote: Writing, checking, answering customers on social, that's literally my job description.
fieldNote: She refuses the tools because using them feels like **training her replacement**.
She hopes **face-to-face work** like sampling is safer, since robots come slowly.
Her progressive views turn quickly into **union talk** and calls for rules.

steps.text: Ask the copy team to meet the creative workers' union
Put fifty a month aside by cutting meals out
Apply for in-store sampling and events jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be furious and loud about it. I'd be signing every petition for a basic income and posting that companies are stealing a whole generation's first jobs. I wouldn't pretend to be calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have no plan at all. Two years is nothing when you have three weeks of savings and no experience anyone wants. My whole job is thinking work, so it hits me on day one, not in 2031 with the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to move back in with my mum, she's two hours away, and give up the flat. I'd take whatever's hands-on and local, café work, warehouse, care work, because those have three more years before robots. And I'd join every protest going, because what else is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like a floor dropping out. I'd feel stupid for having studied this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robots come three years later. Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives café and care jobs a few years, so that's where I'd run. But everyone like me would run there too. Three years of fighting for barista shifts isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum on the phone that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I need my old room back and I don't know for how long. She'd say yes, she always does. That's the part that would make me cry.

say: I'd be **furious**, backing a **basic income** in public.
I'd say companies are **stealing first jobs** from my generation.
think: I think I'd have **no plan at all** with three weeks of savings.
I know my job is all **thinking work**, so it hits me on **day one**.
do: Give up the flat and **move back** to my mum's, two hours away.
Take any **hands-on local job**, like café, warehouse or care work.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing when you have three weeks of savings and no experience anyone wants.
fieldNote: With **two years' warning** she sees no plan and no money to make one.
She sees the **three-year robot gap** as a crowded refuge, not real safety.
Moving home to her **mum** is the only safety net she names.

steps.text: Give up the flat and move back to her mum's
Ask her mum for her old room back
Take café, warehouse or care shifts nearby
Sign petitions and march for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get laws in place and we'd better use them. I'd be pushing the union line hard, slow it down, share the gains. I'd be the annoying one at every family dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years just means I'd watch it coming instead of being hit by surprise. Like I said with the fast one, my job is screen work, so 2031 is my date, not 2034. I might get two or three more pay rises before it ends, if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in something hands-on with people, maybe a teaching assistant qualification, because classrooms feel slower to change. I'd try hard to build a proper cushion, three months, even if it means a cheaper flat. And I'd stay in the union push at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread, but a slower dread. It's like knowing the date of an exam you can't pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A teaching assistant earns less than you do now. Could you live on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely, and not on my own in this city. I'd need a flatmate or my partner Theo's wage. Theo fixes bikes, so he'd be fine longer than me, which is a strange thing to say about a bike mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools at all in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe enough to not get fired before I'm ready to leave. Not because I believe in it. It's more like learning the rules of a game you hate.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to pass laws and should use them.
I'd keep pushing the **union line**: slow it down and share the gains.
think: I think five years just means I **watch it coming**.
My job is screen work, so **2031** is my date, not 2034.
do: Start a **part-time course** to become a teaching assistant.
Build a **three-month cushion**, even if it means a cheaper flat.
Learn just enough of the **AI tools** to keep the job meanwhile.
feel: A slower **dread**, like knowing the date of an exam I can't pass.
S3.quote: Five years just means I'd watch it coming instead of being hit by surprise.
fieldNote: Extra time helps her **plan an exit**, but she still expects to lose the job.
She relies on her partner **Theo's** hands-on work outlasting her desk job.
She would use AI only **reluctantly**, as a holding move, not out of belief.

steps.text: Start a part-time teaching assistant course
Move to a cheaper flat to build three months' savings
Keep pushing the copy team to join the union
Learn the basic AI writing tools only to hold the job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind. I'd want a proper public plan for retraining, paid for by the companies making the money. That's the post I'd write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes a big difference for me. At 37 I'd still be young enough to have a whole second career. I probably wouldn't be in marketing by then anyway, the way I'm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the teaching qualification properly, maybe full-time in a couple of years once I've saved. I'd keep the copy job while it lasts, because the money matters. And I'd keep at the union stuff, because the rules are what decide if it's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it feels like something I could actually steer. I hate that it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd likely not be in marketing anyway. Does that make this easier or harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier, in a sad way. I never felt brilliant at it, Ruth still rewrites half my lines. Maybe the decade just pushes me where I was drifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay in marketing, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they kept real humans on the ideas side, and the pay was decent. I'm not holding my breath for either.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for leaving people behind.
I'd call for a **public retraining plan** paid for by the companies profiting.
think: I think a decade gives me **a second career**, since I'd only be 37.
I probably wouldn't stay in **marketing** anyway.
do: Do a **teaching qualification** properly, full-time once I've saved.
Keep the **copy job** while it lasts for the money.
Stay active in the **union** to shape the rules.
feel: Still **worried**, but it feels like something I could **steer**.
S4.quote: At 37 I'd still be young enough to have a whole second career.
fieldNote: The **ten-year** gap moves her from panic to a plan she controls.
She admits she was already **drifting out** of marketing.
Her progressive view still frames everything as a fight over **who pays**.

steps.text: Train full-time as a teaching assistant in two years
Stay in the copy job for the wage meanwhile
Stay active in the creative workers' union

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question. I'd have no money, no time and no skills anyone wants. What would help is a real income floor while people retrain, and a union with teeth so firms can't just drop juniors overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what it's like to start a career right when it might end. Nobody my age has a picture of being forty in this job. I don't think I have one either.

headlineQuote: Nobody my age has a picture of being forty in this job.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** junior copywriter at an oat-milk brand who drafts everything in a paper notebook.
She has **three weeks** of savings, low pay and few similar jobs in her city.
She refuses AI tools, seeing them as **training her replacement**, and turns to unions and rules instead.
She goes from anxious under AI Plateau to **panicked** with two years' warning, steadier with ten.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, with **no money** or skills to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income floor** while people retrain.
A **strong union** that stops firms dropping juniors overnight.
